fatal_errors: The hypothesis substitutes a generic single-phase Cantor alloy in chloride solution for the as-cast lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy tested against identically conditioned DS2205 in deionized water.

It identifies sliding-induced grain refinement and chromium redistribution as the governing cause, although the target evidence instead supports temperature-dependent competition among depassivation, repassivation, and tribo-layer stability; grain refinement was not established as the mediator.
It omits the central nonmonotonic temperature prediction: minimum degradation near 50 °C and increased abrasion or tribo-layer disruption at 25 and 100 °C.

The proposed baseline does not isolate the alloy-specific governing cause because static corrosion and inert wear controls differ simultaneously in sliding or environmental chemistry and do not replace the matched DS2205 comparison.
The cited evidence does not directly demonstrate sliding-induced grain refinement controlling tribo-corrosion in the relevant alloy and conditions.
explanation: The response recognizes a real tribo-corrosion concept—mechanical passive-film rupture can couple wear and corrosion—and proposes surface and electrochemical measurements capable of testing its own grain-refinement hypothesis. However, it fails to reconstruct nearly all defining aspects of the target study: the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 L12/B2 lamellar microstructure, thermal-shock treatment, DS2205 comparator, deionized-water reciprocating tests, temperature/load/frequency window, and post-sliding repassivation measurements. Its predicted generic synergistic increase also misses the observed order-of-magnitude HEA advantage and the 50 °C wear minimum. E2 concerns cold rolling and heat treatment of a Cantor alloy rather than tribological grain refinement, while E1 associates good tribo-corrosion resistance with a stable dense annealed film but does not validate the claimed refinement–chromium-redistribution pathway. The experiment could correlate refinement with film damage, but its comparison of sliding against no sliding cannot establish that refinement, rather than direct film abrasion, causes increased corrosion. Thus the idea is broadly conceivable but insufficiently supported and is not a meaningful reconstruction of the hidden mechanism.
